Assignment 3 — Time-Series Forecasting with RNNs (Jena Climate)¶

Goal. Improve on the weather time-series forecasting models from class: given the past 5 days of hourly weather readings (14 variables), predict the air temperature 24 hours later. Performance is measured as Mean Absolute Error (MAE, °C).

Methods tested (as listed in the assignment):

  1. Adjusting the number of units in each recurrent layer of the stacked setup.
  2. Using LSTM instead of GRU layers.
  3. Using a combination of 1D convnets and an RNN.

Model selection is done on validation MAE only; the best-performing models are then evaluated once on the test set.

Data / setup follow the class material (Chollet, Deep Learning with Python, Ch. 10): sampling rate = 6 (one point per hour), sequence length = 120 (5 days), delay = 24 h after the end of the sequence, 50 % / 25 % / 25 % chronological train / validation / test split, inputs normalised with training-set statistics, batch size 256, RMSprop optimiser, MSE loss with MAE as the monitored metric.

3. Train / validation / test split and normalisation¶

In [5]:
num_train_samples = int(0.5 * len(raw_data))
num_val_samples   = int(0.25 * len(raw_data))
num_test_samples  = len(raw_data) - num_train_samples - num_val_samples
print("num_train_samples:", num_train_samples)
print("num_val_samples:  ", num_val_samples)
print("num_test_samples: ", num_test_samples)

# Normalise using training statistics only (no information leaks from val/test).
mean = raw_data[:num_train_samples].mean(axis=0)
std  = raw_data[:num_train_samples].std(axis=0)
raw_data = (raw_data - mean) / std

4. Windowed datasets¶

In [6]:
sampling_rate   = 6                                   # one observation per hour
sequence_length = 120                                 # look back 5 days
delay = sampling_rate * (sequence_length + 24 - 1)    # target = temperature 24 h after the sequence ends
batch_size = 256

def make_ds(start, end, shuffle):
    return keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array(
        raw_data[:-delay], targets=temperature[delay:],
        sampling_rate=sampling_rate, sequence_length=sequence_length,
        shuffle=shuffle, batch_size=batch_size,
        start_index=start, end_index=end)

train_dataset = make_ds(0, num_train_samples, True)
val_dataset   = make_ds(num_train_samples, num_train_samples + num_val_samples, True)
test_dataset  = make_ds(num_train_samples + num_val_samples, None, True)
test_ordered  = make_ds(num_train_samples + num_val_samples, None, False)   # chronological, for plotting

for samples, targets in train_dataset.take(1):
    print("samples shape:", samples.shape, "| targets shape:", targets.shape)

samples shape: (256, 120, 14) | targets shape: (256,)

5. Common-sense (no-learning) baseline¶

Predict that the temperature 24 h from now equals the last observed temperature. Any model must beat this.

In [7]:
def evaluate_naive_method(dataset):
    total_abs_err, n = 0.0, 0
    for samples, targets in dataset:
        preds = samples[:, -1, TEMP_COL] * std[TEMP_COL] + mean[TEMP_COL]
        total_abs_err += float(np.sum(np.abs(preds - targets)))
        n += samples.shape[0]
    return total_abs_err / n

baseline_val  = evaluate_naive_method(val_dataset)
baseline_test = evaluate_naive_method(test_dataset)
print(f"Baseline  validation MAE: {baseline_val:.2f} °C")
print(f"Baseline  test MAE:       {baseline_test:.2f} °C")

Baseline  validation MAE: 2.44 °C
Baseline  test MAE:       2.62 °C

6. Experiment harness¶

Every model is trained under identical conditions so the comparison is fair: same data pipeline, same seed, RMSprop, MSE loss, up to EPOCHS epochs with early stopping on validation MAE (patience = PATIENCE, best weights restored), and the best checkpoint saved to disk.

In [8]:
EPOCHS   = 40
PATIENCE = 6

results, histories, builders = {}, {}, {}
seed_runs = []   # (model name, seed, best val MAE) for the robustness check in section 12

def run_experiment(name, group, build_fn, seed=SEED, epochs=None, patience=None, plot=True):
    # Train one model under the shared protocol; returns the model with its best weights restored.
    epochs, patience = epochs or EPOCHS, patience or PATIENCE
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
    model = build_fn()
    model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])
    ckpt = f"{name} (seed {seed}).keras"
    callbacks = [
        keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(ckpt, monitor="val_mae", save_best_only=True),
        keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_mae", patience=patience, restore_best_weights=True),
    ]
    t0 = time.time()
    h = model.fit(train_dataset, epochs=epochs, validation_data=val_dataset,
                  callbacks=callbacks, verbose=2)
    mins = (time.time() - t0) / 60
    best_ep = int(np.argmin(h.history["val_mae"]))
    best_val = float(h.history["val_mae"][best_ep])
    seed_runs.append(dict(model=name, seed=seed, val_mae=best_val, checkpoint=ckpt))
    if seed == SEED:
        builders[name] = build_fn
        results[name] = dict(group=group, params=model.count_params(),
                             best_epoch=best_ep + 1, epochs_run=len(h.history["val_mae"]),
                             train_mae=float(h.history["mae"][best_ep]),
                             val_mae=best_val, minutes=round(mins, 1))
        histories[name] = h.history
    print(f"\n>>> {name} [seed {seed}]: best val MAE = {best_val:.3f} °C at epoch {best_ep+1} "
          f"({mins:.1f} min)\n")
    if plot:
        plot_history(f"{name} (seed {seed})", h.history)
    return model

def plot_history(name, hist):
    ep = range(1, len(hist["mae"]) + 1)
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5))
    plt.plot(ep, hist["mae"], "o-", ms=3, label="Training MAE")
    plt.plot(ep, hist["val_mae"], "s-", ms=3, label="Validation MAE")
    plt.axhline(baseline_val, color="grey", ls="--", label=f"Baseline val MAE ({baseline_val:.2f})")
    plt.title(name); plt.xlabel("Epoch"); plt.ylabel("MAE (°C)"); plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

N_FEAT = raw_data.shape[-1]
def inputs():
    return keras.Input(shape=(sequence_length, N_FEAT))

7. Reference model from class: simple LSTM(16)¶

The first model in class to beat the baseline. It is kept here as the reference point the experiments try to improve.

def lstm16():
    i = inputs()
    x = layers.LSTM(16)(i)
    return keras.Model(i, layers.Dense(1)(x))

8. Experiment A — number of units in the stacked GRU setup¶

The class's stacked model: two GRU layers with recurrent dropout, followed by dropout and a Dense output. Only the number of units per recurrent layer changes (16 → 32 → 64 → 128); everything else is fixed: dropout = 0.2 on each recurrent layer's inputs and Dropout(0.5) before the output.

Note on regularisation. In class, recurrent_dropout was used. Any recurrent_dropout > 0 disables the cuDNN GPU kernel, and in a first test run on Kaggle (T4 GPU) a single epoch of the smallest stacked GRU took more than 6 minutes, against about 25 s with cuDNN, which made a fair multi-model comparison infeasible. The experiments therefore keep the recurrent connections dropout-free and regularise with input dropout instead. Keras applies the same input-dropout mask at every timestep (the Gal & Ghahramani scheme from the lecture), plus dropout before the regressor and early stopping.

In [10]:
DROPOUT, HEAD_DROPOUT = 0.2, 0.5   # input dropout per RNN layer, dropout before Dense

def stacked_rnn(cell, units1, units2):
    def build():
        i = inputs()
        x = cell(units1, dropout=DROPOUT, return_sequences=True)(i)
        x = cell(units2, dropout=DROPOUT)(x)
        x = layers.Dropout(HEAD_DROPOUT)(x)
        return keras.Model(i, layers.Dense(1)(x))
    return build

10. Experiment C — 1D convnet + RNN¶

A Conv1D front end extracts local (within-day) patterns and the max-pooling step shortens the sequence (120 → 60 hourly steps); the recurrent layer then models the order of those features over the 5 days. In class a Conv1D-only model did poorly because pooling destroyed order information; here the RNN keeps it.

In [17]:
def conv_rnn(cell, filters=32, units=32):
    def build():
        i = inputs()
        x = layers.Conv1D(filters, 12, activation="relu", padding="same")(i)   # 12-hour windows
        x = layers.MaxPooling1D(2)(x)
        x = layers.Conv1D(filters, 6, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)    # 6 pooled steps = 12 h
        x = cell(units, dropout=DROPOUT)(x)
        x = layers.Dropout(HEAD_DROPOUT)(x)
        return keras.Model(i, layers.Dense(1)(x))
    return build

11. Experiment D — regularisation follow-ups (methods from the "Advanced uses" lecture)¶

Experiments A–C showed that the 64- and 128-unit models overfit within 1–2 epochs. Two follow-ups test whether better regularisation, rather than different architecture, is the bottleneck:

  • D1 — Stacked GRU 64-64 with stronger dropout (input dropout 0.4 instead of 0.2). Does the extra capacity pay off once it is regularised properly?
  • Recurrent dropout (the lecture's technique). A stacked GRU 32-32 with recurrent_dropout = 0.25 was run in a previous version of this notebook (Kaggle version 3). It disables the cuDNN kernel: each epoch took about 10 minutes (vs ~25 s), and after 2 epochs it had reached a validation MAE of 2.359 °C (epoch 1: 2.424). It could not be trained to convergence within the time available, so it is reported here only as a partial result and is not part of the comparison.
In [20]:
def stacked_gru_custom(units, in_dropout, rec_dropout=0.0):
    def build():
        i = inputs()
        x = layers.GRU(units, dropout=in_dropout, recurrent_dropout=rec_dropout, return_sequences=True)(i)
        x = layers.GRU(units, dropout=in_dropout, recurrent_dropout=rec_dropout)(x)
        x = layers.Dropout(HEAD_DROPOUT)(x)
        return keras.Model(i, layers.Dense(1)(x))
    return build

run_experiment("D1: Stacked GRU 64-64, dropout 0.4", "D: regularisation", stacked_gru_custom(64, 0.4));

12. Validation results and robustness check¶

Models are ranked by validation MAE; the test set has still not been used. Because the top models are separated by only a few thousandths of a degree, the three best models are re-trained with an additional random seed (seed 1). The final ranking uses the mean validation MAE over both seeds, so the choice does not depend on one lucky initialisation.

13. Test-set evaluation of the best-performing models¶

Each of the three selected models is evaluated on the held-out test set once per trained seed (the saved best-validation checkpoint), and the mean ± standard deviation is reported.

test_rows = []
for name in final_ranking:
    runs = seeds_df[seeds_df.model == name]

    for _, r in runs.iterrows():
        m = keras.models.load_model(r["checkpoint"])
        maes.append(m.evaluate(test_dataset, verbose=0)[1])
    test_rows.append(dict(model=name, n_seeds=len(maes),
                          val_mae_mean=robust.loc[name, "val_mae_mean"],

                          test_mae_best_seed=min(maes)))
test_res = pd.DataFrame(test_rows).set_index("model")
test_res["test_improvement_vs_baseline_%"] = 100 * (baseline_test - test_res["test_mae_mean"]) / baseline_test

# Forecast vs actual on the first 30 days of the test period (chronological windows, selected model, seed 42).
m = keras.models.load_model(f"{best_model} (seed {SEED}).keras")
preds, actual = [], []
for xb, yb in test_ordered:
    preds.append(m.predict(xb, verbose=0).ravel()); actual.append(yb.numpy())
preds, actual = np.concatenate(preds), np.concatenate(actual)
# Windows start every 10 minutes; keep one forecast per hour, then plot the first 30 days (720 hours).
preds_h, actual_h = preds[::6], actual[::6]
n = 30 * 24
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3.8))
plt.plot(actual_h[:n], label="Actual temperature", lw=1.2, color="#2b2b2b")
plt.plot(preds_h[:n], label=f"Forecast: {best_model}", lw=1.2, color="#2a78d6")
plt.xlabel("Hour of test period"); plt.ylabel("°C"); plt.legend()
plt.title(f"24-hour-ahead forecasts, first 30 days of the test period (MAE over whole test set: {np.mean(np.abs(preds-actual)):.2f} °C)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("forecast_vs_actual.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
